21.text:
Fast food is sold on almost every high street and advertised as cheap and convenient, and some people say that it is a waste of time and money. I partly agree with this view, since fast food offers poor value for money once health is considered, although it can save time in a busy day.

To begin with, fast food offers poor value for money once health is considered. A meal may be cheap and quick, but it usually contains a lot of salt, sugar and fat and little fibre, and regular eating raises the risk of obesity, diabetes and heart disease, which cost far more later in medical bills and lost working days. A family that eats takeaway meals every evening, for example, may spend twice as much as one that cooks simple dishes at home, and gain less nutrition. Cooking at home with basic ingredients such as rice, beans and vegetables is usually cheaper and healthier, and it takes little more time than queueing for a takeaway.

However, the claim that fast food wastes time is less convincing. For people who work long shifts or have young children, a quick meal can be a sensible solution on a day when there is no time to shop and cook. Eating occasionally at a fast-food restaurant is unlikely to harm a healthy person, and some outlets now offer salads, fruit and smaller portions. The problem is not the food itself but eating it too often. Governments and companies can help by publishing calorie information, reducing salt and sugar and promoting healthier options, so that busy people are not forced to choose between speed and health.

In conclusion, fast food is a poor use of money when eaten regularly, but it can save time in moments of need, so I agree only partly with the statement.

29.text:
Obesity has more than doubled in many countries over the past few decades, and it now affects both adults and children. This essay will analyse the principal causes and propose realistic solutions.

Obesity is caused by an unhealthy balance between the energy people take in and the energy they use. Cheap, energy-dense food is easy to buy and heavily advertised, portions have grown, and sugary drinks add many calories without making people feel full. At the same time, modern life involves long hours of sitting at screens, desks and in cars. A child who spends every evening on a games console and travels to school by car, for example, uses far less energy than children did in the past. In addition, stress, poor sleep and family habits can make the problem worse, and some people are more likely to gain weight because of their genes. As a result, extra weight builds up slowly over years, and in poorer areas fresh food and safe places to exercise can be hard to find.

To address this issue, governments should make healthy eating and activity part of everyday life. School meal standards, daily physical education, limits on advertising of unhealthy food to children and safe play areas shape habits at an age when they are easiest to form. In addition, taxes on sugary drinks, clearer food labels and cheaper fruit and vegetables help adults to choose better, and doctors can offer advice and support before weight becomes a serious problem. A city that builds cycle lanes and parks, for instance, makes exercise easy and enjoyable. These measures cost less than treating diabetes and heart disease.

In conclusion, obesity stems mainly from cheap, heavily marketed food and inactive lifestyles, but school policies, healthier food environments and more active communities offer a realistic way forward.

142.text:
Overweight children are now seen in schools around the world, and they face a higher risk of diabetes, heart problems and low self-esteem. This essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take, focusing on healthy food and activity at school and on changing the wider environment in which children grow up.

To begin with, governments should make healthy eating and activity part of children's everyday lives at school. School meal standards, daily physical education, limits on advertising to children and safe play areas shape habits at an age when they are easiest to form. A school that serves fresh meals and gives every pupil a daily sports lesson, for instance, helps children to build habits that last into adulthood. Vending machines selling sugary snacks can be replaced with water and fruit, and cooking and nutrition lessons can teach children how to prepare simple, healthy meals. Because children spend much of the day at school, these steps reach almost every child, regardless of family income.

In addition, authorities should change the environment outside school and support parents. Taxes on sugary drinks, restrictions on promoting unhealthy products to children and stricter rules on fast-food outlets near schools reduce temptation, while safe parks, cycle lanes and affordable sports clubs make activity easy and enjoyable. Equally important, health workers can give advice and support to families when a child begins to gain weight, and campaigns can help parents to understand portion sizes and screen time. These measures cost much less than treating obesity-related disease in adulthood, and they bring lasting benefits for health and education.

In conclusion, improving school food and exercise and creating a healthier environment for families offer the most realistic way of reducing childhood obesity.

349.text:
Doctors and health campaigns constantly advise people to eat well, and many people say that a healthy diet prevents illness. I largely agree with this view, since good food lowers the risk of many serious diseases, although a healthy diet cannot guarantee good health on its own.

To begin with, a healthy diet lowers the risk of many serious illnesses. Eating plenty of vegetables, fruit and whole grains and little processed food reduces the chance of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers. Such foods supply vitamins, fibre and minerals that keep the body working properly, while diets high in salt, sugar and fat are linked to high blood pressure and obesity. A person who replaces fried snacks and fizzy drinks with fruit, nuts and water, for example, may lower their blood pressure within months and reduce the chance of needing medication later. Good nutrition also strengthens the immune system, so the body fights infections more effectively.

Furthermore, the effect on children can last a lifetime. Children who learn to enjoy balanced meals are likely to carry those habits into adulthood and to avoid weight problems. However, diet is only one factor. Genes, infections, accidents, air pollution and stress also affect health, so a person can eat well and still become ill. Exercise, sleep, avoiding smoking and regular medical checks are equally important. Diet should therefore be seen as an important part of prevention, not a guarantee. People should not blame themselves too harshly when illness occurs despite careful eating.

In conclusion, I largely agree that a healthy diet prevents illness, because it reduces the risk of major diseases, although it works best alongside other healthy habits and cannot remove every risk.

339.text:
Hunger and poor nutrition still hold back millions of children, even in countries that are not poor. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on child nutrition programmes: healthier, better-performing children, and long-term savings and opportunity.

First and foremost, child nutrition programmes help children to grow, learn and stay healthy. Well-fed children concentrate better, attend school more regularly and suffer fewer illnesses, so they are more likely to finish their education. A child who receives a free school breakfast, for example, is less likely to feel tired and distracted in morning lessons. Programmes that provide meals, milk, fruit or vitamins also reduce stunting and anaemia, which can harm a child's development for life. Teachers report that children who eat properly behave better, and parents on low incomes are relieved of a daily worry.

In addition, nutrition programmes bring long-term savings and opportunity. Healthier children grow into healthier adults who work more productively and need less medical care, so the cost of the programme is repaid many times over. Because poor children benefit most, the programmes help to break the cycle of poverty, since education and health are the main routes out of it. They can also support local farmers if schools buy fresh produce from nearby farms, and they teach children about food and cooking. Although providing meals requires organisation and money, careful targeting and local sourcing can keep costs under control. Countries such as Brazil and India have run large school meal schemes, which suggests that this approach is practical.

To sum up, child nutrition programmes bring clear benefits to a country, above all healthier, better-educated children and long-term savings. For these reasons, they deserve sustained public support.

311.text:
Alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs are used by a worrying number of teenagers, and the habit can damage their health and education for years. This essay will analyse the principal causes and propose realistic solutions.

Teenagers turn to drugs and alcohol because of peer pressure, stress and easy access. Friends who use substances make it seem normal, family problems and school pressure create a wish to escape, and curiosity combined with a lack of knowledge about the risks leads some young people to experiment. A fifteen-year-old at a party where everyone is drinking, for example, may accept a drink simply to avoid being left out. In addition, substances are often cheap and easy to obtain, and advertising, films and social media can make them look glamorous. Teenage brains are still developing, which makes young people more impulsive and more vulnerable to addiction. Early use can then develop into dependence and damage health, relationships and exam results.

To address this issue, prevention should combine education, support and strict control of sales. Schools can explain the real risks, and sessions led by former users can be more convincing than warnings from adults. Counselling helps teenagers with stress and family difficulties, and enforcement stops shops from selling to minors. Clubs, sport and youth centres give young people healthy alternatives and a sense of belonging. In addition, treatment services must be available for those who already have a problem, and parents need advice on how to talk to their children without anger. Prevention is far less costly than dealing with addiction later, and it protects the futures of young people.

In conclusion, teenage substance abuse stems mainly from peer pressure, stress and easy access, but education, family support and firm enforcement offer a realistic way forward.

472.text:
Contaminated food can make large numbers of people ill within a few hours, and some argue that stricter food safety regulations protect public health. I largely agree, since strong rules prevent outbreaks and build trust, although they must be fair and enforceable.

To begin with, strict food safety rules protect public health. Inspections, hygiene standards and traceability reduce outbreaks of food poisoning and allow contaminated products to be recalled quickly, which builds trust in the food industry. A restaurant that stores raw meat next to salad, for example, can cause an outbreak of food poisoning that affects dozens of customers. Rules about cooking temperatures, cleaning, storage and labelling of allergens remove many of these risks. Because consumers cannot see bacteria or check a factory for themselves, they depend on regulation to keep food safe, and children, older people and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable.

Furthermore, regulations create a level playing field and support trade. Honest producers are not undercut by careless ones who save money by ignoring hygiene, and exporters need to meet high standards to sell in other countries. After a serious scandal, the damage to an entire industry can be far greater than the cost of prevention. However, strict rules also have costs. Small farmers and local sellers may find paperwork and equipment expensive, and enforcement requires well-trained inspectors. Authorities should therefore apply proportionate rules, give advice and time to small businesses, and focus inspections on the highest risks, so that safety is improved without destroying livelihoods.

In conclusion, stricter food safety regulations protect public health to a large extent, because they prevent illness and build trust, provided that they are proportionate and well enforced.

195.text:
Many countries have banned smoking in restaurants, offices and other public places, and some people believe that these bans improve public health. I largely agree, since they reduce exposure to smoke and help people to quit, although the size of the effect depends on how well the bans are enforced.

To begin with, smoking bans reduce exposure to harmful smoke and encourage people to quit. Second-hand smoke causes heart disease, lung disease and asthma among non-smokers, and when smoking is no longer allowed in public it becomes less normal and harder to continue. A waiter who works eight hours a day in a smoky restaurant, for example, breathes in harmful smoke even though he has never smoked, and a ban removes that risk completely. After bans were introduced in several countries, hospitals reported fewer admissions for heart attacks and breathing problems, which suggests that the policy works. Fewer opportunities to smoke also help smokers who are trying to cut down.

Furthermore, bans protect groups who cannot choose. Children, pregnant women and people with asthma suffer most from smoky air, and employees often cannot avoid it. Bans also change social attitudes, so that young people are less likely to see smoking as normal and start the habit. However, bans cannot work on their own. Smokers who are addicted need support, such as help with quitting and higher taxes on tobacco, and rules must be enforced fairly or they will be ignored. Smoking at home, where children may still be exposed, is also hard to control and needs education rather than law.

In conclusion, public smoking bans improve public health to a large extent by reducing exposure and encouraging quitting, provided that they are enforced and supported by help for smokers.

266.text:
Smoking harms not only the smoker but also the people around, and governments in many countries are deciding how far to restrict it. I agree that governments should ban smoking in public places, since people have a right to breathe clean air, although some flexibility may be needed outdoors.

To begin with, non-smokers have a right to breathe clean air. When smoking is allowed in enclosed places such as restaurants, offices and public transport, people who have not chosen to smoke are forced to inhale harmful smoke, which can cause asthma, heart disease and lung cancer. A waiter who works eight hours a day in a smoky restaurant, for example, breathes in harmful smoke even though he has never smoked, and he cannot easily change jobs. Children are especially at risk, since their lungs are still developing. Public places are shared by everyone, so the right to clean air should take priority over the habit of a few.

Furthermore, bans change habits and save money. They make it easier for smokers to cut down or quit, reduce litter from cigarette ends and lower the healthcare costs of smoke-related illness. Admittedly, a total ban limits personal freedom and may be difficult to enforce, particularly in open areas, and many smokers are addicted rather than careless. However, freedom to smoke does not extend to harming others, and designated outdoor areas, away from entrances and children, can balance the rights of smokers and non-smokers. Fines should be reasonable, and help for people who want to stop smoking should be widely available, so that the policy is seen as fair rather than punitive.

In conclusion, I agree that governments should ban smoking in public places, because it protects non-smokers and improves health, provided that the ban is fair and combined with support for smokers.
